title: Welcoming Shabbat
hook: six psalms for six weekdays, begun by the mystics of Safed who went out to greet the day

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying alone, and Hannah at Shiloh. Your line was alone still counts. Today, the week ends, and the prayer book changes.

Late Friday afternoon, in a hill town in the Galilee, in the 1500s. A group of scholars and mystics put on white clothes and walk out past the last houses, into the fields, as the sun drops toward the sea. They aren't going anywhere. They're going out to meet someone. The town is Safed, home to a famous circle of Jewish mystics, and the someone they're walking out to greet is the Sabbath itself. Almost every synagogue's Friday night service still carries the shape of that walk.
screen: `FRIDAY, IN SAFED.` → `WHITE CLOTHES, INTO THE FIELDS.` → `GOING OUT TO MEET SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Kabbalat Shabbat means receiving, or welcoming, the Sabbath. The idea is old. The Talmud tells of a sage who wrapped himself in his cloak at sundown on Friday and said: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the Queen. But the service with that name took shape in Safed, in the sixteenth century, among the circle of kabbalists there, and from them it spread around the Jewish world. Its backbone is six psalms, ninety-five through ninety-nine, and twenty-nine: one for each of the six weekdays that have just ended. You walk back through the week, psalm by psalm, before you step into the seventh day. The first is a summons. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 95 begins: "O come, let us sing unto the LORD; let us shout for joy to the Rock of our salvation." The last, Psalm 29, is a thunderstorm: the voice of the LORD, seven times over, upon the waters, breaking the cedars, shaking the wilderness. And then it ends with one word: peace. After the storm of the week, peace. Some say the seven voices match the seven blessings of the Friday night Amidah. Then comes a song, which is tomorrow's lesson, and then the two psalms that belonged to Shabbat long before Safed. Notice the posture. Shabbat isn't a day you fall into when you're tired. It's someone you go out to meet, dressed for it, on time.
screen: `GO OUT TO GREET THE QUEEN.` · `SAFED, SIXTEENTH CENTURY.` · `SIX PSALMS FOR SIX DAYS.` · `THE STORM ENDS IN PEACE.` · then, large: `WELCOME THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Look back at your week one day at a time, the way the six psalms do, and take just one image from each day so far. Then, if you'd like, read Psalm 95 or 29 slowly, or simply say its first line, O come, let us sing, and picture yourself walking out to meet the evening.
Kabbalat Shabbat. Welcoming the Sabbath. Six psalms for six days, from the mystics of Safed who walked out to meet it.
Your line: welcome the day. Six psalms behind you, and the seventh day ahead. See you on day six hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Kabbalat Shabbat is the Friday evening service before Maariv in most communities: Psalms 95–99 and 29, the song Lecha Dodi, then Psalms 92 and 93. Many congregations sing it, and some still begin it outdoors.

chat.says: Why do Friday night services start with a string of psalms?
options: Six psalms for the six weekdays, walking back through the week to greet Shabbat.
They're psalms of mourning for the Temple, said before the joy of Shabbat.
They're the psalms read at weddings, since Shabbat is greeted as a bride.
